A Mohist came from the north, claiming to have a strategy to save the world. Yan Guang heard of this and eagerly invited him into the manor.
Initially, the Mohist entered the manor, acting arrogantly, repeatedly presenting strategies to Guang. Unaccepted, he wished to leave. Then Yan Guang made a pact with the Mohist: if he could recreate the legendary craftsman De Heng's puppet that could spin for ten days without stopping, his advice would be heeded. The Mohist agreed and completed it in over a month. On the ninth day of spinning, it still hadn't stopped. On the tenth day, the Mohist requested funds to prepare for the Yellow River canal. Yan Guang laughed heartily, then led the Mohist to see—the mechanism had malfunctioned and collapsed. The Mohist, suspicious, inspected it and found a wooden peg that didn't fit. Yan Guang made another pact: if the Mohist could drink a hundred jars of wine in the manor, his strategy would be accepted.
How foolish and laughable! Who knows if that Mohist drank all hundred jars?
Did Yan Guang truly wish to save the world? He merely sought to impress the emperor and regain favor!
Did the emperor truly wish to save the world? By submitting to the Khitans, neither seeking profit nor provoking conflict, he merely sought fame in history!
Did the Mohist truly wish to save the world? To save the world with clever tricks—such a thing has never been heard of!
Now observe: all are but clowns jumping for fame and profit, playing games with us common folk. National policy? People's policy? World policy? What good does it do you? What good does it do me? Like a dream, it's but a joke.
